title: Cantar de mio Cid
titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Toward Valencia: Murviedro taken, the Moors of Valencia routed (tiradas 64–68, lines 1085–1155)
part: Tiradas 64–68 · Toward Valencia: Murviedro taken, the Moors of Valencia routed (lines 1085–1155)
source: Ramón Menéndez Pidal (ed.), Poema de mio Cid, 2.ª edición corregida (Clásicos Castellanos 24; Madrid: Ediciones de “La Lectura”, 1923), pp. 199–203, lines 1085–1154 (tiradas 64–68). Text follows Pidal's critical text exactly, including its old accentuation and mixed spellings; Pidal's italics (his editorial restorations) are shown in [brackets], and a line he restores whole is flagged in its note. Line numbers are Pidal's. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed twelfth-century Castilian. Translations made fresh from the Old Spanish; Pidal's notes and vocabulary (1908–11) the lexical aids.

sentences.t: Aquis conpieça la gesta de mio Çid el de Bivar.
sentences.l: Here-itself begins the deed-song of my Çid he of Bivar.
sentences.i: Here begins the song of the deeds of my Çid, he of Vivar.
sentences.n: Cantar segundo · Bodas de las hijas del Cid ('Second Cantar · The Weddings of the Cid's Daughters'): Pidal's heading. With this line the second of the poem's three cantares opens; there is no heading in the poem's own text: the line's words announce the new start. Tirada 64 (assonance á) — the Çid moves against the lands of Valencia (Pidal: El Cid se dirige contra tierras de Valencia). The line-ends are a stressed á (Bivar, Alucat, ducá, Alván, guerrear, part, Almenar, ha). The count runs 1085, 1087: Pidal prints line 1086 (tan ricos son los sos que non saben qué se an) at the end of tirada 63, where the previous part closed, and sets this opening line at the head of the new cantar; his numbers are kept. Aquis = aquí se, 'here (it) begins', the se squeezed onto aquí as -s. conpieça = comienza. gesta, 'deeds', and the song that tells them.

sentences.t:
Poblado ha mio Çid el puerto de Alucat,
dexado [h]a Saragoça e a las tierras ducá,
e dexado [h]a Huesa e tierras de Mont Alván.
sentences.l:
Settled has my Çid the pass of Alucat,
left he-has Saragoça and the lands of-here,
and left he-has Huesa and lands of Mont Alván.
sentences.i: My Çid has settled in the pass of Alucat; he has left Zaragoza and the lands on this side, and left Huesa and the lands of Montalbán.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1087: as a result of the victory over the count of Barcelona, the Çid settles for good in the lands of the king of Lérida (compare vv. 958, 951, and his introduction, pp. 15–16). Poblado ha, dexado [h]a: aver + past participle, the participle put first; poblar, 'to settle, occupy'. [h]a, the h Pidal's (in italics) in both lines. puerto, 'mountain pass'. dexado = dejado. ducá: read here as d'acá, 'of this side', the lands on the near side; Pidal gives no note on the page and the reading is uncertain. Huesa is a town of Teruel, not Huesca; Mont Alván = Montalbán.

sentences.t:
Contra la mar salada conpeçó de guerrear;
a orient exe el sol, e tornós a essa part.
sentences.l:
Toward the sea salt he-began to make-war;
at east goes-out the sun, and turned-himself to that side.
sentences.i: Toward the salt sea he began to wage his war: the sun rises in the east, and that way he turned.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1090: contra means 'hacia', 'toward'; it does not mean that the Castilian hero is able to 'make war against the sea itself', as Más y Prat took it (1885). conpeçó de guerrear, 'began to make war' (comenzar de + infinitive). exe = sale, 'goes out, rises' (exir, as exida at v. 11). tornós = tornó se, the se squeezed on. The Çid turns from Aragon toward the Mediterranean, where the sun comes up.

sentences.t:
Myo Çid gañó a Xérica e a Onda e Almenar,
tierras de Borriana todas conquistas las ha.
sentences.l:
My Çid won Xérica and Onda and Almenar,
lands of Borriana all conquered them he-has.
sentences.i: My Çid won Jérica, Onda and Almenara; the lands of Burriana he has conquered, every one.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1092: Jérica, Onda, Almenara and Burriana are towns of the south of the province of Castellón, bordering on Valencia. About 1091 the Cid was living at Burriana; but Almenara he took only about 1098, that is, after Valencia had been conquered (so far Pidal). The poem thus gathers into one campaign conquests spread over several years. Myo, so spelled here. gañó = ganó; a before the place-names. conquistas = conquistadas, a short participle agreeing with tierras; las takes up the object put first: 'he has them conquered'.

sentences.i: The Creator helped him, the Lord who is in heaven. With all this he took Murviedro; now my Çid saw that God was standing by him.
sentences.n: Tirada 65 (assonance é-o) — the taking of Murviedro (Pidal: Toma de Murviedro). The line-ends are é-o (çielo, Murviedro, valiendo, miedo). Ayudól = ayudó le, 'helped him'. Criador, 'the Creator', God. es en çielo, 'is in heaven', ser of place. priso, 'took', old strong preterite of prender. Pidal's note to v. 1095: Murviedro, 29 km north of Valencia, was conquered by the Cid only after that city, in 1098 (compare the note to v. 1092). vi[d]íe = veía, the old imperfect vidíe, the d Pidal's (in italics). iva valiendo, ir + gerund; valer, 'to help, protect'.

sentences.t: Dentro en Valençia non es poco el miedo.
sentences.l: Within in Valençia not is little the fear.
sentences.i: Inside Valencia the fear is no small one.
sentences.n: Dentro en, 'within'. non es poco, 'is not small', an understatement for 'great'. The present after the preterites priso and vidíe: the poem's tense-mixing. Valencia, the great Moorish city on the coast, is the goal of this cantar.

sentences.t:
Pesa a los de Valençia, sabet, non les plaze;
prisieron so consejo quel viniessen çercar,
sentences.l:
It-weighs to those of Valençia, know-ye, not to-them it-pleases;
they-took their counsel that-him they-should-come to-besiege,
sentences.i: It weighs on the people of Valencia — be sure of it, they are not pleased; they took counsel to come and besiege him.
sentences.n: Tirada 66 (assonance á) — the Moors of Valencia besiege the Çid; he gathers his men; his address (Pidal: Los moros valencianos cercan al Cid. Éste reúne sus gentes.—Arenga). The line-ends are a stressed á (plaze, çercar, man, fincar, maravillar, spirital, mal, pan, fazen, partirá …, ending at durar, escarmentar); in plaze, fazen and salve (1115) the unstressed last syllable does not count. pesa a, 'it weighs on, grieves'. sabet = sabed, 'know', the minstrel's aside to his hearers. so = su, here 'their'. quel = que le, 'that him'. viniessen çercar, venir + bare infinitive, 'come to besiege'.

sentences.t:
Trasnocharon de noch, al alva de la man
açerca de Murviedro tornan tiendas a fincar.
sentences.l:
They-passed-the-night-marching by night, at-the dawn of the morning
near of Murviedro they-turn tents to pitch.
sentences.i: They marched through the night, and at the dawn of morning, close by Murviedro, they set about pitching their tents.
sentences.n: Trasnocharon, 'they spent the night on the move', a night march (trasnochar). noch = noche. al alva de la man, 'at the dawn of the morning', man cut short from mañana. açerca de, 'near'. tornan … a fincar, 'they turn to pitching': fincar here 'to plant, fix' (f- for h-: hincar). Preterite trasnocharon, then present tornan: tense-mixing again.

sentences.t:
Viólo mio Çid, tomós a maravillar:
“Grado a tí, Padre spirital!
sentences.l:
Saw-it my Çid, took-himself to marvel:
“Thanks to thee, Father spiritual!
sentences.i: My Çid saw it, and he fell to marvelling: “Thanks be to thee, spiritual Father!
sentences.n: Viólo = vió lo, 'saw it'. tomós = tomó se: tomarse a + infinitive, 'to set to, begin'. maravillar, 'to marvel'. Line 1102b is a single half-line, printed in roman type (it is in the manuscript, not a restoration of Pidal's); it carries a b-number so that the traditional count from 1103 on is undisturbed, and Pidal gives no note on it on the page. Grado a tí, 'thanks to thee', as at v. 8. Padre spirital, 'the spiritual Father', God. The Çid gives thanks at the sight of the enemy's tents: the speech that follows shows why.

sentences.i: We are in their lands and do them every harm; we drink their wine and eat their bread: if they come to besiege us, they do it by right.
sentences.n: femosles = femos les, 'we do to them' (femos = hacemos, f- for h-). tod mal, 'every harm', tod cut short from todo. so vino, el so pan: so = su, 'their'; el so pan, article + possessive, as las sus bocas. nos çercar vienen, the pronoun drawn up before the verbs. con derecho, 'by right, justly': the Çid grants the enemy his case.

sentences.t: A menos de lid aquesto nos partirá;
sentences.l: Without battle this us will-part;
sentences.i: Short of a battle, this will not be settled between us;
sentences.n: a menos de lid, 'without a battle' (lid, 'battle'), as a menos de batalla at vv. 983 and 989. aquesto = esto. partir, 'to part, separate', here 'to settle, decide'. As it stands the line has no negative ('without a battle this will part us'); the sense the context asks for, and the parallel of v. 983 (a menos de batalla non pueden den quitar), is 'this will not be settled for us without a battle'. Pidal gives no note, and the exact construction is uncertain.

sentences.t:
vayan los mandados por los que nos deven ayudar
los unos a Xérica e los otros a Alucad,
desí a Onda e los otros a Almenar,
los de Borriana luego vengan acá;
sentences.l:
let-go the messages for those who us must help
the ones to Xérica and the others to Alucad,
thence to Onda and the others to Almenar,
those of Borriana at-once let-them-come here;
sentences.i: let messages go out to those who are bound to help us, some to Jérica and others to Alucat, then to Onda, and others to Almenara; let the men of Burriana come here at once;
sentences.n: vayan, 'let (them) go', subjunctive of command. mandados, 'messages' (or the messengers who carry them). los que nos deven ayudar: the garrisons of the places just won (vv. 1087–1093). los unos … los otros, 'some … others'. Alucad = Alucat of v. 1087, ending in d here. desí, 'thence, then'. luego, 'at once' (in Old Spanish, not 'later').

sentences.t:
conpeçaremos aquesta lid campal,
yo fío por Dios que en nuestro pro eñadrán.”
sentences.l:
we-will-begin this battle of-the-field,
I trust by God that in our profit they-will-add.”
sentences.i: we shall join this pitched battle; I trust in God that they will add to our gain.”
sentences.n: conpeçaremos = comenzaremos. aquesta = esta. lid campal, 'battle in the open field', a pitched battle. fío por Dios, 'I trust in God'. Pidal's note to v. 1112: eñadir or añadir en algo, 'to increase something': 'aumentarán nuestro provecho', 'they will increase our profit'. pro, 'profit, advantage'. The subject of eñadrán is not named: most naturally the men summoned, though not certain. eñadrán = añadirán, a syncopated future (eñadirán > eñadrán).

sentences.t:
Al terçer día todos juntados s’[a]n,
el que en buen ora nasco compeçó de fablar:
sentences.l:
At-the third day all gathered themselves-have,
he who in good hour was-born began to speak:
sentences.i: On the third day they have all gathered, and he who was born in a good hour began to speak:
sentences.n: juntados s'[a]n = se han juntado, 'they have gathered', the participle first and agreeing with todos; the a of an (= han) is Pidal's (in italics). el que en buen ora nasco, the standing formula, 'he who was born in a good hour'. compeçó, written with m here (conpeçó elsewhere). fablar = hablar, f- for h-.

sentences.t:
“Oíd, mesnadas, sí el Criador vos salve!
Después que nos partiemos de la linpia cristiandad,
—non f[o] a nuestro grado ni nos non pudiemos mas,—
grado a Dios, lo nuestro f[o] adelant.
sentences.l:
“Hear, troops, so the Creator you save!
After that we parted from the clean Christendom,
—not was-it at our will nor we not could more,—
thanks to God, the ours went forward.
sentences.i: “Hear me, my companies, so may the Creator save you! Since we parted from pure Christendom — not by our own will, nor could we do otherwise — thanks be to God, our fortunes have gone forward.
sentences.n: mesnadas, 'household troops, companies'. sí el Criador vos salve, 'so may the Creator save you': sí (accented) is 'so', with a wishing subjunctive, not si 'if'. partiemos, pudiemos = partimos, pudimos, old preterites in -iemos. linpia cristiandad, 'clean, pure Christendom', the Christian lands they left. f[o] = fue, in both lines the o Pidal's (in italics). a nuestro grado, 'by our will'. ni nos non pudiemos mas, 'nor could we do more', i.e. had no choice, with the double negative ni … non. Pidal's note to v. 1118: grado a Dios, 'gracias a Dios', 'thanks be to God' (v. 792). lo nuestro, 'what is ours', our affairs; adelant, 'forward'.

sentences.i: The men of Valencia have besieged us; if we mean to hold on in these lands, these men must be taught a hard lesson.
sentences.n: çercados nos han = nos han cercado, the participle first, agreeing with nos. quisiéremos, future subjunctive after si. durar, 'to last, stay on'. firme mientre = firmemente: the adverb ending -mente is still a separate word (mientre). son … a escarmentar, ser a + infinitive, 'are to be punished': escarmentar, 'to punish so that it is not tried again'. The speech does not end here: it runs on into the next tirada.

sentences.i: Let the night pass and the morning come: be ready for me with horses and arms; we will go and see that host of theirs.
sentences.n: Tirada 67 (assonance á-a) — end of the Çid's address (Pidal: Fin de la arenga del Cid). The line-ends are á-a (mañana, armas, almofalla, estraña, soldada). The speech begun at v. 1115 carries on across the change of assonance: a new tirada, not a new speaker. se[e]d = sed, 'be', imperative of seer, ser; the second e is Pidal's (in italics), as in ve[e]r, the old two-syllable veer, 'to see'. me, 'for me', the speaker's interest. Pidal's note to v. 1124: 'atacaremos aquel su ejército', 'we will attack that army of theirs' (v. 1224): 'go and see' is 'go at'. almofalla, 'host, encampment' (Arabic al-maḥalla). aquella su, demonstrative + possessive.

sentences.t:
Commo omnes exidos de tierra estraña
allí pareçrá el que mereçe la soldada.”
sentences.l:
As men gone-out from land foreign
there will-appear he who deserves the pay.”
sentences.i: As men gone out from their own land into a strange one, there it will be seen who earns his pay.”
sentences.n: exidos = salidos, 'gone out', the exiles (compare el salido at v. 980). de tierra estraña: the phrase is loose, 'men gone out of the land, in a foreign land' or 'men come out of a foreign land'; Pidal gives no note, and the exact sense is uncertain, though the point is plain: the exiles live by what they win. pareçrá = parecerá, a syncopated future, 'will appear, be seen'. soldada, 'wages, pay' of a retained man: compare ir nos hemos pagando at v. 1046.

sentences.t:
Oíd qué dixo Minaya Álbar Fáñez:
“Campeador, fagamos lo que a vos plaze.
sentences.l:
Hear what said Minaya Álbar Fáñez:
“Campeador, let-us-do what to you pleases.
sentences.i: Hear what Minaya Álvar Fáñez said: “Campeador, let us do what pleases you.
sentences.n: Tirada 68 (assonance á) — Minaya gives the battle plan; the Çid wins another pitched battle; the taking of Cebolla (Pidal: Minaya da el plan de batalla. El Cid vence otra lid campal.—Toma de Cebolla). The line-ends are a stressed á (Fáñez, plaze, más, delant, avrá, part, será, armar, far, va, voluntad, Bivar, crebar, reconbrar, arrancar, escapar, alcaz …, ending at far, van); in Fáñez, plaze, Yague, tendales and traen the unstressed last syllable does not count. Oíd, the minstrel turning to his hearers. Minaya Álbar Fáñez, the Çid's right hand, here spelled Álbar. Campeador, 'the Battler', the Çid's title. fagamos = hagamos, f- for h-.

sentences.t:
A mí dedes çient cavalleros, que non vos pido más;
vos con los otros firádeslos delant.
sentences.l:
To me may-you-give hundred knights, for not you I-ask more;
you with the others may-you-strike-them in-front.
sentences.i: Give me a hundred knights — I ask you for no more; you, with the rest, strike them from the front.
sentences.n: dedes = deis, a subjunctive as a polite request. çient = cien. que, 'for'. firádeslos = los firades (hiráis), subjunctive of ferir, 'strike them', the pronoun glued on. delant, 'in front, head-on'.

sentences.t:
Bien los ferredes, que dubda non i avrá,
yo con los çiento entraré del otra part,
commo fío por Dios, el campo nuestro será.”
sentences.l:
Well them you-will-strike, for doubt not there will-be,
I with the hundred will-enter from-the other side,
as I-trust by God, the field ours will-be.”
sentences.i: You will strike them hard, there will be no doubt of it; I with the hundred will go in from the other side, and, as I trust in God, the field will be ours.”
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1131: ferredes, 'heriréis', 'you will strike'; a combined attack (his introduction, p. 98). ferredes is the future of ferir with the i dropped (ferirédes > ferredes). dubda = duda. i avrá = habrá, 'there will be'. del otra part, 'from the other side' (del before a feminine noun, as el amistad). el campo, 'the field': to hold it is to win.

sentences.t: Commo gelo a dicho al Campeador mucho plaze.
sentences.l: As it-to-him he-has said to-the Campeador much it-pleases.
sentences.i: Now that he has said it to him, the Campeador is greatly pleased.
sentences.n: Commo, 'as, when'. gelo = se lo, 'it to him' (ge for le before lo). a dicho = ha dicho, the h-less spelling. plaze, 'it pleases'.

sentences.t:
Mañana era e piénssanse de armar,
quis cada uno dellos bien sabe lo que ha de far.
sentences.l:
Morning it-was and they-think-themselves to arm,
each every one of-them well knows what he-has to do.
sentences.i: It was morning, and they set about arming; every one of them knows well what he has to do.
sentences.n: piénssanse de armar, 'they set about arming' (pensar de + infinitive, with se). quis cada uno dellos: read here as 'each and every one of them', quis (Latin quisque, 'each') strengthening cada; Pidal gives no note on the page, the form is rare and the analysis is offered with caution. dellos = de ellos. ha de far, 'has to do', far = fazer cut short.

sentences.t:
Con los alvores mio Çid ferirlos va:
“¡En el nombre del Criador e d’apostol santi Yague,
feridlos, cavalleros, d’amor e de voluntad,
ca yo so R[o]y Diaz, mio Çid el de Bivar!”
sentences.l:
With the dawn-lights my Çid to-strike-them goes:
“In the name of-the Creator and of-apostle saint James,
strike-them, knights, of love and of will,
for I am Roy Díaz, my Çid he of Bivar!”
sentences.i: At first light my Çid goes to strike them: “In the name of the Creator and of the apostle Saint James, strike them, knights, with love and with a will, for I am Ruy Díaz, my Çid of Vivar!”
sentences.n: alvores, 'first light' (albores). ferirlos va, ir + infinitive, 'goes to strike them', he attacks. santi Yague, 'Saint James' (Santiago), the battle-cry of Christian Spain; d'apostol, d'amor, de with the vowel cut before a vowel. feridlos = heridlos, f- for h-. d'amor e de voluntad, 'with love and good will', with all their hearts. so = soy. R[o]y, only the o Pidal's (in italics). Pidal's note to v. 1140: the leader shouted his name to hearten his men (see v. 721). The Çid calls himself mio Çid, the epithet now his battle-name.

sentences.t:
Tanta cuerda de tienda i veriedes [cr]ebar,
arrancarse las estacas e acostarse a todas partes los tendales.
Moros son muchos, ya quieren reconbrar.
sentences.l:
So-much cord of tent there you-would-see break,
pull-up-themselves the stakes and lean-themselves to all sides the poles.
Moors are many, now they-want to-recover.
sentences.i: So many tent-ropes you would have seen snapping there, the stakes torn up and the poles leaning over on every side! The Moors are many; now they try to rally.
sentences.n: veriedes = veríais, 'you would see', the minstrel's appeal to his audience. [cr]ebar = quebrar, 'to break', the cr Pidal's restoration (in italics). Pidal's note to v. 1142: acostarse los tendales, 'ladearse, caerse los postes', 'the poles on which the tents are pitched lean over and fall'; the same description of an assault on the Moorish camp recurs at v. 2400. Pidal's note to v. 1143: reconbrar, 'recobrar', 'to recover'. Being many, the Moors try to regain their footing. ya quieren, 'now they are trying'.

sentences.i: From the other side Álvar Fáñez broke in upon them; grieve as it might, they had to give way and flee, those who could get away at the full gallop of their horses.
sentences.n: entróles = entró les, 'came in on them'. Pidal's note to v. 1145: maguer les pesa, 'aunque les pesa', 'though it grieves them' (compare v. 3116). oviéronse a dar e a arrancar: aver a + infinitive, 'had to'; dar(se), 'to give way'; arrancar, 'to be routed, flee' (the rout is the arrancada). Print order: the numbers follow the manuscript, and from here Pidal rearranges the lines, printing 1145, 1151, 1147–1149, 1152, 1153, 1146, 1150, 1155, 1154; his numbers are kept, and the text follows his print. He gives no note on the reordering on these pages. Pidal's note to v. 1151: de pie[de]s de cavallo, 'a uña de caballo', at full gallop; piedes = pies, the de Pidal's (in italics). ques = que se.

sentences.t:
Dos reyes de moros mataron en es alcaz,
fata Valençia duró el segudar.
sentences.l:
Two kings of Moors they-killed in that pursuit,
up-to Valençia lasted the pursuing.
sentences.i: Two Moorish kings they killed in that pursuit; all the way to Valencia the chase went on.
sentences.n: es = ese, 'that' (as es logar at v. 1146). alcaz, 'pursuit' (from alcançar). fata = hasta. segudar, 'to pursue', the infinitive used as a noun, 'the chase'.

sentences.i: Great are the gains my Çid has made; they plundered the field and turned for home. They came into Murviedro with the winnings they bring, and great is the joy that runs through that town.
sentences.n: fechas ha, 'has made', fechas agreeing with ganançias (as conquistas las ha at v. 1093). robavan el campo, 'they stripped the field' of its spoil. piénssanse de tornar, 'they set about returning'. Imperfect, present and preterite run together (robavan, piénssanse, entravan, traen): epic tense-mixing. es logar = ese lugar. 1146 (grand es el gozo) stands in the manuscript right after 1145; Pidal moves it here, after the return to Murviedro, presumably so that the rejoicing follows the return; he gives no reason on the page.

sentences.i: They took Cebolla and all that lies beyond it; in Valencia they are so afraid they know not what to do; the tidings of my Çid, be sure of it, are ringing far and wide.
sentences.n: Pidal's note to v. 1150: Cebolla is a popular etymology of the vulgar Arabic diminutive jubayla, 'little hill' (cebolla is Spanish for 'onion'); today it is called el Puig (podium, 'hillock') and lies some 18 km north of Valencia; the Cid took this Puig or Cebolla in 1093. quanto que es i adelant, 'all that is there onward', i = 'there'. an = han, 'they have'. que no saben qué se far, 'so that they do not know what to do', far = fazer. Pidal's note to v. 1154: nuevas, 'renombre, fama', 'renown, fame' (compare vv. 1556, 1206, 2084). sonando van, ir + gerund, 'go sounding'. Printing 1155 before 1154, Pidal ends the tirada on the Çid's fame, which the next tirada takes up in its first words (Sonando van sus nuevas, v. 1156).
